content: 1. The threshold for red blood cell folate levels can serve as an indicator of folate insufficiency in women of reproductive age. However, no specific serum folate threshold is recommended for the prevention of neural tube defects at the population level for this demographic. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of microbiological assays as the most reliable method for obtaining comparable red blood cell folate results across different countries. 3. Daily iron supplementation is advised as a public health intervention for menstruating adult women and adolescent girls in areas with a high prevalence of anemia (40% or higher). This is aimed at preventing anemia and iron deficiency. 4. Intermittent iron and folic acid supplementation is recommended for menstruating women in regions with a high prevalence of anemia (20% or higher) to improve hemoglobin levels, iron status, and reduce the risk of anemia. 5. Daily iron supplementation is also recommended for school-age children (60 months and older) in areas with a high prevalence of anemia to prevent iron deficiency and anemia. In malaria-endemic areas, iron supplementation should be paired with public health measures to prevent, diagnose, and treat malaria. 6. Intermittent iron supplementation is recommended for preschool and school-age children in areas where anemia prevalence is 20% or higher to improve iron status and reduce anemia risk. 7. Routine use of multiple micronutrient powders during pregnancy is not recommended as an alternative to standard iron and folic acid supplementation for improving maternal and infant health outcomes. 8. Vitamin A supplementation in postpartum women is not recommended for preventing maternal and infant morbidity and mortality. 9. WHO considers a population prevalence of gestational anemia of 20% or higher to be a moderate public health problem. 10. Management of severe acute malnutrition in school-age children, adolescents, and adults, including pregnant and lactating women with active tuberculosis, should follow WHO recommendations for severe acute malnutrition management. 11. For individuals with moderate undernutrition and active tuberculosis who fail to regain normal body mass index after two months of treatment or lose weight during treatment, adherence and comorbid conditions should be evaluated. Nutritional assessment, counseling, and provision of nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods may be necessary. 12. Pregnant women with active tuberculosis and moderate undernutrition or inadequate weight gain should receive nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to achieve a minimum weekly weight gain of approximately 300 grams during the second and third trimesters. 13. Patients with active multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and moderate undernutrition should be provided with nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to restore normal nutritional status. 14. Efforts to prevent adolescent pregnancy and poor reproductive outcomes should include interventions to delay marriage until at least 18 years of age, increase educational opportunities for girls, and provide comprehensive sexuality education and contraceptive services. 15. Interventions to reduce adolescent pregnancy rates should combine curriculum-based sexuality education with contraceptive promotion and ensure access to postpartum and post-abortion contraception. 16. Efforts to increase contraceptive use among adolescents at risk of unintended pregnancy should include policy changes to improve access, community engagement to support contraceptive use, and health service delivery improvements. 17. Interventions to reduce coerced sex among adolescents should include legal and policy measures to punish perpetrators, empower victims, and enhance adolescent girls' self-esteem, life skills, and social support networks. 18. Efforts to reduce unsafe abortion among adolescents should ensure access to safe abortion services, provide information about legal options, and address barriers to service provision. Post-abortion care should be accessible as a life-saving intervention. 19. Pregnant adolescents should be informed about the importance of skilled antenatal, childbirth, and postnatal care. Birth preparedness and emergency readiness should be promoted, and access to emergency obstetric care should be expanded. 20. Counseling on healthy eating and physical activity during pregnancy is recommended to prevent excessive weight gain and maintain maternal health. 21. In undernourished populations, nutrition education to increase daily energy and protein intake is recommended to reduce the risk of low-birth-weight neonates. Balanced energy and protein dietary supplementation is also recommended to reduce the risk of stillbirths and small-for-gestational-age neonates. 22. High-protein supplementation is not recommended for pregnant women to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. 23. Daily iron and folic acid supplementation is recommended for pregnant women to prevent maternal anemia, puerperal sepsis, low birth weight, and preterm birth. Weekly supplementation may be considered in populations with low anemia prevalence if daily supplementation is not acceptable due to side effects. 24. Calcium supplementation is recommended for pregnant women to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia, particularly in populations with low dietary calcium intake. 25. Vitamin A supplementation is only recommended for pregnant women in areas where vitamin A deficiency is a severe public health problem to prevent night blindness. 26. Zinc supplementation for pregnant women is only recommended in the context of rigorous research. 27. Multiple micronutrient supplementation is not recommended for pregnant women to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. 28. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) supplementation is not recommended for pregnant women to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. 29. Vitamin E and C supplementation is not recommended for pregnant women to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. 30. Vitamin D supplementation is not recommended for pregnant women to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. 31. Pregnant women with high daily caffeine intake (more than 300 mg per day) are advised to reduce their caffeine consumption to lower the risk of pregnancy loss and low-birth-weight neonates. 32. Vitamin A supplementation in HIV-positive pregnant women is not recommended as a public health intervention to reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV. 33. Birth preparedness and complication readiness interventions are recommended to increase the use of skilled care at birth and timely facility care for obstetric and newborn complications. 34. Male involvement interventions during pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum are recommended to support improved self-care, home care practices, and use of skilled care for women and newborns. These interventions should respect women's autonomy and decision-making. 35. Dialogue with traditional birth attendants, women, families, and communities is recommended to define alternative roles for traditional birth attendants in supporting maternal and newborn health. 36. Lay health workers, including trained traditional birth attendants, are recommended for promoting maternal and newborn health behaviors and services, providing social support during labor, and administering misoprostol to prevent postpartum hemorrhage. 37. Ongoing dialogue with communities is essential to define culturally appropriate, quality maternity care services that address the needs of women and newborns.
